title: A lamp on a stand (Mark 4:21–25)
hookLine: light isn't meant to hide under a bowl

cards: It's getting dark in a one-room house in Galilee. Someone fills a small clay lamp with olive oil, lights the wick, and then, very carefully, puts a bowl over it. Or slides it under the bed.
Everyone would laugh. That's the joke Jesus tells next, so obvious it sounds silly: nobody lights a lamp to hide it. Lamps are easy.
Other kinds of light get hidden more quietly: a gift kept back, a belief never mentioned, a kindness nobody is meant to see.

teach.h: A LAMP, A BOWL, A BED.
teach.b: In the King James Bible: "Is a candle brought to be put under a bushel, or under a bed? and not to be set on a candlestick?" Candle there means an oil lamp, a little clay dish with a spout for the wick.
A bushel is a grain measure, a household bowl. A candlestick is a lampstand, a ledge or stand that lifts the light so the whole room gets it. The Greek has a small oddity.
The sentence literally says: does the lamp come? As if the lamp walked in by itself.
Some readers hear Jesus hinting at himself: the light that has come into the room is not meant to stay hidden for long. Then he says nothing is hidden except to be revealed later.
After yesterday, it sounds like a promise: what the twelve heard in private is meant to come out into the open.

Then a warning about listening, which ties back to the sower: "Take heed what ye hear: with what measure ye mete, it shall be measured to you: and unto you that hear shall more be given." Mete means measure out.
Whoever pays attention is given more to pay attention to. Christians have taken the lamp two ways, often both at once. Some hear it about the good news, which isn't a secret to hoard.
Others hear it about their own lives: whatever light they've been given, faith, a gift, kindness, is meant for the room, not a bowl. Not to show off. Just so people can see.

how: Christians often read the lamp as a call to live their faith openly and to use what they've been given for others.

o: a torch carried on a night journey
a small clay oil lamp with a wick
a tall stand that holds up a light

games.q: what the old words mean — tap the pairs.

s: the candle in the story was a wax candle
it was a small clay oil lamp with a wick.

games.q: it's dark and you've just lit your only lamp. where do you put it?
o: under a bowl, to keep it safe.
under the bed, out of the way.
games.why: on the stand, of course. that's the joke: nobody lights a lamp to hide it.

practice: Ask yourself what's under your bowl: maybe you draw, or sing in the car, and nobody knows; maybe you pray and never mention it, or quietly fix things at work, or care about someone and have never said it.
Choose one, and picture lifting the bowl and setting that light where someone can see it, not to be admired, just to help the room. If you pray, you can offer it to God.

wordCard.voice: Candle, the King James word for a small oil lamp, never meant to be hidden under a bowl or a bed, but lifted onto a stand.

orig.note: Greek: a small portable oil lamp. The King James calls it a candle.

carryVoice: Your line: put it on the stand. Nobody lights a lamp to hide it. Until tomorrow.
